justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from a current baseline around 412–413, which appears consistent with a broad equity index (likely the S&P 500 or a similar benchmark) trading in that neighborhood. For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed level, adding only a small positive drift since daily moves tend to revert toward recent trends, and near-term momentum appeared mildly constructive. For the one-week estimate, I extended that drift slightly, reflecting the historical tendency for equity markets to grind modestly higher over short periods when no major macro disruptions are immediately visible. For the one-month estimate, I pushed the point estimate a bit further, incorporating a longer-run equity risk premium effect while acknowledging that one month is still a short enough window that mean-reversion forces don't dominate dramatically.

The confidence interval widths were set to reflect typical realized volatility at each horizon. Daily equity index volatility tends to run around 0.8–1.2% in normal regimes, which translates to a fairly tight band for the one-day interval. As you extend to one week, volatility scales with the square root of time, so uncertainty compounds, widening the interval meaningfully. At one month, the uncertainty band roughly doubles relative to one week given that same scaling logic, and I additionally widened it slightly to account for the possibility of regime shifts or macro surprises that are more likely to materialize over a longer window.

Specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these intervals include a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — particularly labor market or inflation prints — that forces a repricing of Federal Reserve policy expectations. A geopolitical shock, credit event, or significant earnings miss from a heavily weighted index constituent could also generate a move that breaks through the lower bound of even the one-month interval. On the upside, a surprisingly dovish central bank pivot or a resolution of ongoing trade or geopolitical tensions could drive a sharp rally beyond the upper bounds I stated.

It is also worth noting that liquidity conditions and market microstructure can occasionally amplify moves in ways that pure volatility models understate. Thin trading periods, options expiration dynamics, or forced de-leveraging events are fat-tail risks that my intervals do not fully capture, since they were calibrated primarily around a normal-to-slightly-fat-tailed distributional assumption. Tail events occurring within any of these horizons remain genuinely possible and represent the primary reason actual outcomes could fall meaningfully outside the stated 90% confidence intervals.
